sections.h2: Where does a deed get recorded in Morrow County?
sections.html:
Morrow County deeds and mortgages are recorded at the county recorder's office inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St., Mt. Gilead, OH 43338. The recorder's page lists 419-947-3060 and counter hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Mount Gilead is the county seat and the largest village in the county, so most sellers who live in Cardington, Marengo, Edison or the townships make the same trip. Anyone who prefers not to drive can file through an electronic recording company instead (see below).

sections.h2: What kinds of documents does the Morrow County recorder accept?
sections.html:
The office's documents-filed list is broad. For a home sale or an inherited house, these are the entries you are most likely to need:

  • Deeds, including warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages, along with releases, assignments, assumptions and subordinations.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Liens of several kinds, such as mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominium filings, annexations and zoning resolutions also appear on the list, which tells you the same office holds the map side of the county's land records.

sections.h2: Can a Morrow County deed be filed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The recorder's page says e-recording has been open for every document type since September 8, 2025, and it names four vendors to call for help: CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm. Title companies and closing attorneys usually already hold an account with one of them, so a seller rarely needs to sign up personally.

Record searching moved to a different system in the same period. The records search page sends visitors to RecordHub, where you must create a login before you can look anything up. The county says the account costs nothing and that the login requirement was added to protect the records from cyberattacks.

sections.h2: What happens at the auditor's office before the recorder sees the deed?
sections.html:
Under section 319.20, the county auditor moves the parcel into the new owner's name and endorses the deed. Before that happens, the buyer or the buyer's representative files a statement of value as described in section 319.202, electronically or in three paper copies.

The statement carries two questions that matter to a Morrow seller. Has the property received a tax reduction for owner-occupied homes? And was the land ever enrolled in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program? If the answer to the second is yes, the statement must note that the land can face a recoupment charge when it stops qualifying.

The Morrow County Auditor's own conveyance fee page prints $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The grantor pays it, together with the 50 cent transfer fee that section 319.54(G)(2) sets for each parcel entered.

sections.h2: What does Ohio charge to record a document?
sections.html:
The recorder has no room to set its own prices for the basic filing. Section 317.32 prescribes a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee, and the recorder may also add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars that goes to the county general fund. Payment is due when the paper is handed in, though electronic filers may settle afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method.

Recording charges printed in Ohio Revised Code 317.32

A long deed with several exhibits therefore costs more than a two-page one. Ask the title agent for a page count before closing so the check is the right size.

sections.h2: Which Morrow County transfers owe no conveyance fee?
sections.html:
Section 319.54(G)(3) lists many transfers that skip the auditor's fee. The ones that come up most often in family and estate sales are these:

  • A deed that only corrects or confirms one already recorded.
  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or between a parent and a child or the child's spouse.
  • A transfer among the heirs or devisees of one decedent where no money changes hands.
  • A deed into a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke it, and the deed back out.
  • Any transfer with no money or other valuable consideration that is not a gift.
  • A transfer made only to secure or release a debt.

When an exemption applies, the filing states the reason for it. Anyone unsure whether a family deed qualifies should phone the auditor before the paperwork goes to the recorder.

sections.h2: Who has to sign a Morrow County deed, and how is it witnessed?
sections.html:
Ohio's section 5301.01 requires the grantor to sign the deed and to acknowledge the signature before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. In practice most sellers use a notary at the title company or a bank.

If a mortgage is being paid off from the sale, the lender's release has its own clock. Under section 5301.36, the mortgagee must record the release within ninety days of satisfaction. Check the recorder's index a few weeks after closing to confirm it appears.

sections.h2: How can a Morrow County owner watch for fraudulent filings?
sections.html:
The recorder's office offers a free fraud alert service called Property Check. A subscriber is told when a document is filed against a named property, which helps catch a forged deed or a bogus lien early. The service is a good fit for an owner of a vacant or inherited house, where nobody is watching the mail.

Alerts do not replace a periodic look at the record. A quick RecordHub search under your own name every so often costs only the time it takes to log in.

sections.h2: What is Morrow County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Morrow County sits in central Ohio on about 406 square miles of land and was organized in 1848 from parts of four neighboring counties. It borders Crawford, Richland, Knox, Delaware and Marion counties and belongs to the Columbus metro area. The villages are Cardington, Chesterville, Edison, Fulton, Marengo, Mount Gilead and Sparta, and a slice of the city of Galion reaches in from the north. Ohio's center of population fell near Marengo in 2010, and the Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course draws visitors near Steam Corners.

The Census QuickFacts page for Morrow County lists 36,305 residents in the 2025 estimate and 14,981 housing units. Owner-occupied homes make up 81.2 percent of the stock, the median owner-occupied value is $222,300 for 2020 to 2024, and the mean commute is 32.8 minutes. Houses here are mostly lived in by their owners, and many buyers drive to jobs outside the county.

faqs.q: Who do I call to record a deed in Morrow County?
faqs.a: Call the Morrow County recorder at 419-947-3060. The office is in the courthouse at 48 E. High St. in Mt. Gilead and posts hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.

faqs.q: Does Morrow County accept deeds filed online?
faqs.a: Yes, through electronic recording vendors. The recorder's page names CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm and says e-recording has covered all documents since September 8, 2025.

faqs.q: What is the Morrow County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The county auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office, along with a 50 cent per parcel transfer fee set by state law.

faqs.q: Do I need an account to search Morrow County land records online?
faqs.a: Yes. The records search now runs through RecordHub, and the county asks users to create a free login. The county explains that the step protects the records from cyberattacks.

faqs.q: Is a deed between family members free of the conveyance fee?
faqs.a: Some are. State law exempts gifts between spouses and between a parent and child, and transfers among heirs of one decedent for no money. The filing must state the exemption, so check with the auditor first.
